> **What this case shows** — as a muscle holds a heavy load and tires, the
> ecosystem recovers the textbook **myoelectric fatigue signature**: the EMG
> power spectrum slides toward lower frequencies, so its **median frequency**
> falls over the 120-second hold. Across the cohort the median frequency drops
> from **63.3 Hz to 58.2 Hz** (a **final/initial ratio of 0.92**), in **14 of
> 15** subjects. **What reproduces, and what doesn't** — the *decline* reproduces
> and is what fatigue research keys on; the **absolute** frequency numbers do
> **not** transfer, because this recording was sampled at only 200 Hz with a
> 50 Hz notch sitting inside the EMG band, which shifts where the median lands.
> One subject (**sub4**) barely fatigues — reported, not hidden. **How to read
> it** — left, one subject's median frequency trending down through the hold;
> right, every subject's fatigue index (final ÷ initial frequency), with 1.0
> meaning "no fatigue".

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — answer *"is this muscle fatiguing, and by how much?"* in three
moves: **window** the EMG through the sustained effort → **track** the spectrum's
median frequency window by window → **summarise** the change with a final-vs-initial
index.
**Way of thinking** — fatigue is a *trend within one recording*, not an absolute
number: read the direction and size of the median-frequency shift, and trust it
because a fixed acquisition (sampling rate, notch) cannot manufacture a downward
slope. Report the subjects who don't fatigue rather than averaging them away.
**Ecosystem usage** — chain one function per role, I/O → analysis
(`PhysioExperiment` → `emgFatigue` → `emgFatigueIndex`), letting the shared data
model carry the signal between steps. The final section turns this into a
step-by-step you can adapt to your own EMG.
:::

## Proposition

On real 120-second sustained-contraction surface EMG, the power-spectrum
**median frequency (MDF) falls** over the hold — cohort mean final/initial ratio
**0.918**, an **8.2 %** drop from **63.3 Hz** to **58.2 Hz** — the classic
myoelectric fatigue signature, present in **14 of 15** subjects.

## Question & goal

**The question comes from the dataset's own design.** This dataset (Ebied et al.,
2021) was collected for one purpose: to **analyse upper-limb muscle fatigue from
multi-channel surface EMG**. Fifteen healthy subjects held a **6 kg** load with
the elbow flexed to 90° for **120 seconds** — a protocol designed to *drive the
muscle into fatigue* — while eight EMG channels recorded the effort. The
physiology the protocol targets is well established: as a muscle fatigues, motor
unit conduction velocity slows and firing patterns change, and the EMG power
spectrum **compresses toward lower frequencies** — a *decrease* in its median
frequency over time (De Luca, 1984). So we ask the dataset's own question: does
the ecosystem recover that fatigue signature, and does it hold across the cohort
rather than in a single lucky trace?

## Challenge & approach

Median frequency is noisy window to window, and its absolute value depends on the
acquisition (sampling rate, filtering) — so fatigue must be read as a **trend
within each recording**, not an absolute Hz value compared across setups. The
recipe windows each channel through the hold, computes the spectrum's median
frequency per window, and reduces the whole time course to one number — the ratio
of the final to the initial median frequency:

```
PhysioExperiment(raw = time × 8 channels, sr = 200)  →  emgFatigue()  →  emgFatigueIndex()
```

`emgFatigue()` produces the median-frequency time course (the left panel);
`emgFatigueIndex()` collapses it to a **fatigue index** (final ÷ initial median
frequency, < 1 = fatigue) per channel, which we average over the eight channels
per subject and then across the cohort. Because the pipeline is deterministic
(FFT-based, no randomness), the numbers replay exactly.

## Data

**Multi-channel Surface EMG Dataset for Fatigue analysis** (Ebied et al., 2021) —
public on Zenodo (<https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5189275>), CC-BY-4.0. Fifteen
healthy subjects, **8-channel** surface EMG at **200 Hz** (50 Hz notch),
**6 kg** load at 90° elbow flexion, **120 s** sustained isometric contraction.
The exact archive used is listed in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json). *Ebied A, Awadallah
AM, Abbass MA, El-Sharkawy Y. Upper Limb Muscle Fatigue Analysis Using
Multi-channel Surface EMG. 2020 NILES, 423–427. doi:10.1109/NILES50944.2020.9257909.*

## Results

![Left: for the representative subject (sub15), the channel-averaged EMG median frequency trends downward through the 120 s hold (orange = linear fit). Right: the fatigue index (final ÷ initial median frequency) for all 15 subjects; 14 fall below the 1.0 "no-fatigue" line, one (sub4) sits on it.](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* the fatigue index is each subject's final median frequency
divided by its initial one, averaged over the eight channels — below 1 means the
spectrum shifted down (fatigue), and how far below 1 is how much.

**Cohort summary** ([`artifacts/fatigue_cohort.csv`](artifacts/fatigue_cohort.csv)):

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Subjects with a median-frequency decline (index < 1) | **14 of 15** |
| Mean fatigue index (final ÷ initial MDF) | **0.918** |
| Mean median-frequency change over the hold | **−8.2 %** |
| Mean initial → final median frequency | **63.3 Hz → 58.2 Hz** |
| Mean channels showing a decline (of 8) | 6.7 |

**Spread across subjects**
([`artifacts/fatigue_per_subject.csv`](artifacts/fatigue_per_subject.csv)): the
decline ranges from **−18.4 %** (sub13, index 0.816) down to essentially flat at
**+0.1 %** (sub4, index 1.001, the one non-fatiguing subject). The representative
trace above (sub15, **−7.9 %**, slope **−0.051 Hz/s**) is the subject closest to
the cohort mean.

At the cohort level the median frequency compresses downward under the sustained
load — the myoelectric fatigue signature — recovered end-to-end from the public
recordings.

## Conclusion

On real sustained-contraction EMG the ecosystem reproduces the classic fatigue
signature: as the muscle tires, the spectrum's median frequency falls, in 14 of
15 subjects and by ~8 % on average. The transferable lesson is to read fatigue as
the **direction and size of a within-recording frequency shift** — robust to the
acquisition — rather than as an absolute frequency, and to report the subjects
who don't fatigue instead of averaging them into a tidy mean.

## Open questions

One subject (sub4) shows essentially no median-frequency decline under this
6 kg / 120 s load (index 1.001). Whether that reflects lower relative effort,
genuine fatigue resistance, or electrode placement cannot be resolved from a
single recording — documented, not escalated to a research question.

## Using this in your own analysis

This case is a worked example of **spectral fatigue tracking** — the pattern for
any "is this muscle fatiguing, and by how much?" question.

**The general recipe** (three steps, the same for any fatigue analysis):

1. **Get your EMG into the data model** — build a `PhysioExperiment` from your
   time × channels matrix (or read it with the matching `read*` function), setting
   the sampling rate.
2. **Track the median frequency** through the effort with `emgFatigue()`, which
   windows each channel and returns the spectrum's median and mean frequency per
   window.
3. **Summarise the shift** with `emgFatigueIndex()` — the final ÷ initial median
   frequency (below 1 = fatigue) — and read the *trend*, not the absolute Hz.

**Which functions, and how they compose.** Each step is one ecosystem function,
picked by *role* — I/O → analysis:

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| put a signal matrix into the data model | `PhysioExperiment()` | PhysioCore |
| windowed median/mean-frequency time course | `emgFatigue()` | PhysioEMG |
| final-vs-initial fatigue index per channel | `emgFatigueIndex()` | PhysioEMG |

They chain because `emgFatigue()` and `emgFatigueIndex()` both consume the same
`PhysioExperiment` — the shared data model is what lets the tools snap together,
so you compose the analysis by naming the steps, not by reshaping matrices
between them.

**Choosing the parameters.**

- **`window_sec` / `overlap`** — a ~0.5–1.0 s window with 50 % overlap trades
  spectral resolution against how finely you track the trend; widen it for a
  smoother, slower estimate.
- **`initial_pct` / `final_pct`** (in `emgFatigueIndex()`) — the fractions of the
  hold that define "initial" and "final"; the 20 % default compares the first and
  last fifth, which is robust to the ragged start/end of a contraction.
- **Sampling rate and filtering set the frequency band.** Here 200 Hz sampling
  caps the spectrum at 100 Hz and a 50 Hz notch sits inside it, so the absolute
  median frequency is acquisition-specific — read the *shift*, and prefer ≥ 1 kHz
  sampling when you can, to keep the full EMG band.

**Applying it to your own hypothesis.** Swap in your own sustained-effort EMG,
keep the window → median-frequency → index recipe, and compare the fatigue index
across muscles, loads, or before/after an intervention. The same "trend within a
recording" logic underlies the amplitude side of fatigue (`emgAmplitudeFeatures()`
for RMS/ARV creep) and the synergy-level view of coordinated muscle activity
([`emg-synergy-grabmyo`](../emg-synergy-grabmyo/)).

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioCore); library(PhysioEMG)

# 1. put an 8-channel EMG matrix (time × channels) into the data model
pe <- PhysioExperiment(
  assays = S4Vectors::SimpleList(raw = emg_matrix),   # e.g. read.table("sub1.txt")
  samplingRate = 200)

# 2. track the spectrum's median frequency through the sustained hold
ft <- emgFatigue(pe, window_sec = 1.0, overlap = 0.5) # median_freq per channel per window

# 3. collapse to a fatigue index (final / initial MDF; < 1 = fatigue)
fi <- emgFatigueIndex(pe)                             # one row per channel
mean(fi$fatigue_index)                                # cohort/subject: < 1 means the muscle fatigued
```

**Auditing the numbers.** For readers who want to verify rather than trust: the
per-subject fatigue indices, the cohort summary, and the representative time
course live in [`artifacts/`](artifacts/), and `audit.py` re-derives every number
on this page — including the 14-of-15 count and the cohort means — from those
files.
